title: Government watchdog warns of waste in ICE detention spending
text:
Government watchdog warns of waste in ICE detention spending
A government watchdog says Immigration and Customs Enforcement needs to improve its budgeting as it rapidly expands detention space.
Congress gave Immigration and Customs Enforcement a big allowance to expand detention space. Now, the agency needs better budgeting, a federal watchdog says.
Last year, ICE scored $45 billion to scale up immigrant detention – a key step in the deportation pipeline. A report released last week by Congress’ nonpartisan Government Accountability Office (GAO) found ICE needs more accurate and updated spending plans. Those will help budget for when current coffers run dry, government analysts said.
For one, a warehouse spending spree was “implemented rapidly and will likely result in significant waste,” according to the report. ICE didn’t provide any analysis of cost effectiveness for that plan, the GAO said.
Congress gave Immigration and Customs Enforcement billions of dollars to hold more immigrants as a step toward mass deportation. The agency moved so quickly to spend this money that it did not always consider the longer-term financial consequences.
Under this administration, ICE bought 11 warehouses for around $1.07 billion to expand bed space, but now plans to sell seven. The Trump administration has also faced heaps of litigation tied to those sites, often over environmental reviews.
At existing detention centers, ICE has paid for more beds than are filled, due to guaranteed payments. From October 2025 through April 2026, the report said, ICE had to pay for a daily average of 9,733 empty beds. The GAO previously found that the rushed opening of Camp East Montana in Texas – a collaboration with the U.S. Army – resulted in “millions of dollars of waste.”
ICE plans to dedicate any remaining detention funds from last year’s historic boost by the end of fiscal year 2027 – two years short of how long that funding was meant to last, the GAO said. That plan might limit what ICE can spend on facility maintenance and operations if it continues to burn through so much so fast.
Yet plans to buy alternative facilities now might also present risk, if the need for those beds is reduced, said the GAO. As Democrats take control of Congress, the future of President Donald Trump’s mass-deportation agenda – and need for more beds – is unclear. ICE held more than 65,700 people in detention as of July.
The Department of Homeland Security, which includes ICE, agreed with the report’s recommendations. Those involve ICE’s timely updates on spending plans and development of long-term cost estimates for detention sites.
Related policies are already in place, the government replied. “ICE will continue to monitor detention-fund execution.”
Meanwhile, Trump officials have dismissed mounting claims of poor detention conditions, including allegations of insufficient medical care, excessive use of force, and spoiled food. Other federal investigators have documented such concerns in previous reports.
“ICE is totally out of control,” U.S. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat in line to be House speaker, said last week before the report’s release. The agency’s funding boost “should be redirected.”
